strengths: The paper addresses a useful practical NLP question: how many additional labels make adapting a smaller model preferable to prompting a larger one. Comparing learning curves and break-even points provides more actionable evidence than comparisons at a single training size.

The broad training-size sweep, additional measurements near crossings, and 100 repetitions for most configurations are substantial strengths. Reporting both means and standard deviations exposes instability that single-run comparisons would miss.

Appendix B provides model identifiers, prompts, optimization settings, and decoding details, alongside a source-code link. The training-schedule ablations and explicit discussion of computational and evaluation limitations improve transparency.
weaknesses: The BoolQ prompt in Table 1 asks whether the passage contains an answer to the question, rather than asking the model to answer the question with Yes or No. A passage can contain an answer whose value is No. This changes the task, particularly for zero-shot evaluation, and requires corrected experiments before the BoolQ break-even points or their interpretation through task complexity are reliable.

The evaluation does not establish independence from prior task supervision. Flan-T5's instruction training includes GLUE/SuperGLUE tasks, yet benchmark overlap is not audited. Pooling available labeled examples and creating new 80:20 splits can move original training examples into evaluation. Consequently, the striking ten-label result needs qualification as additional adaptation of an already supervised model, plus evaluation on demonstrably held-out data. SST-2 also requires checking whether related phrases from the same source sentence cross splits.

Label accounting and model selection are insufficiently controlled for the paper's central question. The limitations section explicitly describes choosing prompts using 1,000 test samples. Early stopping and extensive instruction-tuning configuration selection are reported without identifying an independent validation set or its label budget. The nominal zero- and ten-label results therefore do not establish the total supervision required to obtain those configurations.

The variance-adjusted break-even analysis lacks a calibrated statistical interpretation. Non-overlap of mean ± one standard deviation does not establish that fine-tuning 'always' performs better or guarantee a specified failure probability. Moreover, evaluating larger models on 1,000 examples while other models use the full test set mixes different amounts of evaluation uncertainty; six ChatGPT runs also provide much weaker precision than 100 runs. Paired comparisons on common test examples and uncertainty estimates for the crossings would better support this central contribution.

Instruction-tuning uses 150 steps with batch size four, exposing the model to at most 600 example presentations regardless of the nominal dataset size. Thus, the flat curves at thousands of available labels cannot establish that instruction-tuning benefits little from additional training data, and Appendix C's statement that it uses the whole available set is misleading. The analysis should distinguish available labels, examples actually consumed, and optimization budget.

Several numerical interpretations need verification. Figure 2 places an undefined 'Random Baseline' around 70% macro-F1 for SST-2 and 60% for MRPC/BoolQ, which does not correspond to ordinary random binary prediction. Appendix C also describes approximately 900 to 1,200 labels as a 140% increase, although it is roughly 33%. Together with the evaluation issues above, these problems prevent a sound Findings recommendation without corrected experiments and analysis; revision for the next cycle appears feasible.
